question: Using the customary setting of the mathematics used for quantum mechanics, is it possible to prove the existence of Gödelßs god-like entities?

1.text:
In the formal meta-theory which is normally used for QM the derivation can be
written down, not that it gives you anything physical.

The ordinary mathematical background of non-relativistic and relativistic
quantum theory is ZFC + ordinary analysis, i.e. the theory of complex
separable and non-separable Hilbert spaces, unbounded self-adjoint
operators, spectral measures etc.  ZFC can interpret first order logic,
classical second order logic and the normal normal modal logic S5 in which
Gödel's ontological argument is phrased.  In that sense the five
Gödelian axioms

P1. Necessarily, if a property is positive then its negation is not
    positive,
P2. Necessarily, if a property is positive then its necessary
    existential instantiation is positive,
P3. Necessarily, a property is positive iff its converse is positive,
P4. If a property is positive then necessarily it is positive,
P5. Existence is a positive property,

and the definition
G := λx. ∧_{P} P x
can be formalised in the language of ZFC and the usual S5 frame.  On
those premises S5 proves

⊢ □◊∃x Gx → ∃x Gx

and with the usual modal bridge principles one gets the familiar
conditional theorem

⊢ ∃x Gx
in S5 + P1–P5.

That is just a formal theorem of classical modal logic.  It is exactly
the same formal status as the formalisation of the argument in Peano
arithmetic.  The mathematics of Hilbert space does not add any
empirical content to the five positivity axioms nor does it provide a
semantic justification for the S5 necessity operator.  In particular the
axioms P1–P5 are not theorems of analysis, of the spectral theorem, of
C*–algebra theory or of quantum logic; they are substantive metaphysical
principles about the class of "positive" properties.  Hence the
derivation is conditional on accepting those principles, and the
principles themselves are not provable, nor falsifiable, in the
operational content of quantum mechanics.

In the physical interpretation of quantum theory the meaningful logic of
propositions about a quantum system is the orthomodular lattice of
projections in a Hilbert space, quantum logic, not classical S5, and the
positivity axioms have no operational meaning.  So there is no proof, in
the sense of a theorem of the physical theory of quantum mechanics, that
a real god-like maximally positive entity exists.  The formal derivation
is available in the set-theoretic metatheory that underlies the
mathematics of QM, but it remains a purely conditional, stipulative,
formal exercise.  That is the usual way of putting the matter: Gödel's
argument is formally valid in the usual metatheory, it is not a
physical proof of existence. ∎

2.text:
In the usual physics book the mathematics that is actually used is

* ZF/C set theory with the usual analysis,
* complex separable Hilbert spaces $H$, the lattice $P(H)$ of closed
subspaces, the $*$–algebras of bounded operators on $H$ etc.

That is ordinary classical mathematics. Gödel’s ontological argument is
a derivation in first order modal logic $S5$ plus a set of substantive
axioms about a predicate $P$ “is positive”.

In the metalanguage of ZF/C you can of course give a set-theoretic
possible-worlds semantics for $S5$, define a predicate $P$ on the
formal vocabulary $\{G(x),\dots\}$ and reproduce the derivation

$\;{\rm Pos}(E)\land\ldots\vdash\exists x\,\Box\forall y[G(y)\to y=x]$

that Gödel writes down. In that purely syntactic sense the proof can be
written down in the same set theory that is used to formulate the
Spectral Theorem, Stone–von Neumann, etc. The derivation is then a
theorem of the metatheory conditional on the axioms

* $P(\varphi)\to \Box P(\varphi)$,
* $\Box(\varphi\to\psi)\to [P(\varphi)\to P(\psi)]$,
* $P(\exists x\,\varphi(x))\leftrightarrow P(\varphi(c))$,
* $P(E)$ where $E(x)$ is “$x$ exists”,
* etc.,

together with the definition of a god-like thing
$G(x)\equiv \forall\varphi[P(\varphi)\to \varphi(x)]$.

That is exactly what is usually meant by “the proof is formally valid”.
It is not a theorem of quantum mechanics. The axioms are metaphysical
axioms about positivity, necessity and essence; they are not
definable in terms of vectors, projections or observables, and they are
not empirically testable. In particular the proof needs the ordinary
classical, distributive propositional calculus that underlies ZF/C.

If the logic of the theory is taken in the Birkhoff–von Neumann sense,
i.e. the orthomodular lattice $P(H)$ of quantum propositions, the
classical distributive law on which the $S5$ derivation is usually
presented fails. In quantum logic the modal–ontological derivation does
not go through, and there is no physical content to the statement
$\exists x\,G(x)$ in the theory of observables. In the only
physically meaningful sense the existence of a Gödel god-like entity is
not a consequence of, nor is it provable from, the Hilbert-space
mathematics of quantum mechanics; at best it is a conditional formal
derivation in the classical metatheory that one uses to write down the
theory. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. In the customary mathematical setting of quantum mechanics one works in ordinary ZFC-set theory with complex Hilbert spaces, operators, spectral theory and the usual first-order classical logic that underlies functional analysis. That formalism does not carry an intrinsic S5 modal apparatus.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a modal argument: it requires a bona fide necessity operator □ satisfying the S5 axioms and a Kripke frame in which the usual modal notions of necessity and possibility are interpreted. The Hilbert-space lattice of closed subspaces is orthomodular, not Boolean, and the logical connectives that are native to the quantum formalism are those of quantum logic, not the classical propositional logic on which Gödel’s axioms for divine perfection are formulated.

One can of course talk about Kripke models externally, but those models are not part of the mathematics actually used to state, compute and verify quantum mechanical predictions. Within the standard Hilbert-space formalism there is no internal interpretation of “x is necessarily positive” that validates the S5 bridge principles Gödel uses, so the ontological derivation cannot be carried out as an internal theorem of the mathematical language of quantum mechanics. Hence existence of Gödel’s god-like entities cannot be proved in that customary setting.

5.text:
In the ordinary mathematical meta-language in which Hilbert space quantum
mechanics is written down the argument can be written down, but it is not a
consequence of the physical formalism.

The customary mathematical language of non-relativistic quantum mechanics is
first order set theory with the usual structure of a separable complex Hilbert
space H, bounded self-adjoint operators on H and the spectral calculus.
That is ordinary classical mathematics: ZFC plus classical first order
logic. In that meta-language Gödel’s ontological axioms

* P is positive,
* if P is positive then necessarily P is positive,
* if P implies Q then P is positive only if Q is positive,
* Existence is positive,
* Necessarily, a property is positive only if it is consistent,
* Godlike =def the conjunction of all positive properties,

can be formalised and the usual S5 derivation

Necessarily Godlike implies Necessary Existence

is a formal theorem of classical modal logic plus the above axioms.  In
that sense the proof is a piece of ordinary mathematics and it can be
expressed in the same set–theoretic language that is used to define the
Hilbert–space formalism.

What is not supplied by the Hilbert space / C*-algebraic formalism of
quantum mechanics is any physical or mathematical justification for the
positivity axioms, nor the modal ontological principle that
‘positive → necessarily positive’ is a theorem of physics.  The logic
which is physically meaningful inside the theory is not classical
Boolean modal logic at all, but the orthomodular quantum logic of
projections on H.  Classically valid principles such as the full excluded
middle and the S5 modal schemata that Gödel’s derivation uses are not
theorems of the propositional calculus of quantum mechanics, and the
positivity axioms are metaphysical axioms about properties of beings, not
theorems about states, observables or spectra. Hence the existence of a
Godlike being is not a theorem of quantum mechanics; at best it is a
formal consequence of Gödel’s extra-physical axiomatic system, which can
be transcribed – vacantly – in the same classical mathematics that one
uses to talk about Hilbert spaces. The physical theory itself gives no
support for the premises.

3.text:
In the ordinary textbook formalism the mathematics that is used for quantum mechanics is
classical mathematics. A separable complex Hilbert space H, the algebra B(H) of bounded
operators, spectral theory, etc., are all defined in ZFC + Analysis. In particular the
first order language of set theory with the usual arithmetical apparatus is more than
enough to code S5 modal propositional logic and to code Gödel’s list of axioms for
positivity.

Formally therefore Gödel’s ontological argument can be written up inside the same
background set theory which underlies the Hilbert space formalism. What you get is
the usual conditional derivation

A1. P is positive → □P is positive
A2. P→Q → ¬P ∨ Q is positive
...
A5. Existence is positive

then in S5

∃x Gx → □∃x Gx , Gx→□Gx etc.

and under the usual S5 axioms one indeed derives □∃x Gx. That is to say the
statement “a being which has every positive property necessarily exists’’ is a
theorem of the modal theory once the five positivity axioms are granted.

The derivation is therefore not a matter of physics at all. It is a purely
syntactic consequence of the chosen axioms. What it gives you is not a physical
existence claim but the formal consistency statement

Consistent(S5+Gödel axioms) → ⊢ □∃x Gx

in the same set-theoretic metatheory in which H is defined. In particular it
gives no warrant that a “God-like’’ entity exists in the external world, and the
quantum mechanical formalism, which is the same classical mathematics plus the
non-commutative lattice of closed subspaces of H, adds no new ontological
power. The axioms about what counts as positive and about the modal
interaction of necessity and implication are not part of the physical theory and
are notoriously contentious.

In the usual philosophical sense this is therefore not a proof of existence at
all. Moreover, on the usual reading the existence of a necessarily existent
being is essentially the statement of the consistency of the system in which it
is formulated. By Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem a sufficiently strong,
recursively axiomatizable system such as the one that can talk about H and about
arithmetic cannot prove its own consistency internally, so there is no internal
non-conditional proof of a necessarily existent being within the customary
mathematical setting of quantum mechanics. The at best formal derivability of
Gödel’s argument is a logical curiosity, not a physical proof.

9.text:
In the mathematics that is actually used when one does ordinary quantum
mechanics the Hilbert space ${\cal H}$ over ${\mathbf C}$, the $C^{*}$–algebra
of observables, the spectral theory etc., is interpreted in the ordinary
classical metatheory ZFC + classical first order logic + the usual analysis
of the real and complex numbers.  In that metatheory you can formalise
first order modal logic $S5$, you can formalise the set of properties
$P$ and the usual Gödel axioms

* $P$ is closed under entailment,
* if $P\in P$ then $\neg P\notin P$,
* $\Phi\in P\;\to\;\Box\Phi\in P$,
* $\exists x\,\Phi(x)\in P$,

together with the conventional S5 axioms for $\Box$ and you can then
formalise Gödel’s argument

$\exists x\,\Phi(x)\in P$, $\Phi\in P\Rightarrow\Box\Phi\in P$ etc. $\;\vdash\;
\Box\exists x\,G(x)$, and in $S5$

$\Box\exists x\,G(x)\to\exists x\,\Box G(x)$,

so that in the formal system you get the familiar conditional theorem

$G(x)\equiv \forall\Phi\,[\Phi\in P\leftrightarrow\Phi(x)]$ implies
$\Box\exists x\,G(x)$ and hence $\exists x\,\Box G(x)$.

In other words the ontological argument is a purely syntactic theorem of
the classical modal logic in which functional analysis is written down.
It is provable in the same ZFC + PA + analysis that underlies the
Hilbert-space formalism, and in that purely formal sense it is “available’’
to the quantum mechanic.  It is of course a conditional derivability: it
is a theorem relative to the highly contentious metaphysical axioms about
positivity, about the closure of $P$ under $\Box$, and about the
identification of $G(x)$ with the being that has all positive properties.
Changing the background mathematics to the usual complex Hilbert space
adds no new ontological content and does not make the axioms true in the
physical world.

If the quantum content is taken seriously, the propositions of ordinary
quantum mechanics are generally taken to form an orthomodular rather than
a Boolean lattice.  Classical distributivity and the classical $S5$ modal
scheme used by Gödel are not validated by that quantum logical structure,
so the Gödel argument does not survive a literal quantum-logical
interpretation of necessity and of conjunction/disjunction of properties.
In the substantive, physically meaningful sense there is therefore no new
proof of the existence of a Gödel god-like being supplied by the
formalism of quantum mechanics; at best you can write the classical
modal proof down inside the classical mathematics that is the ordinary
metatheory of Hilbert spaces.  That formal derivability is not a physical
or metaphysical proof of the existence of God.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. 

The mathematics that is actually customarily used for quantum mechanics is the ordinary classical formalism of functional analysis: separable complex Hilbert spaces, bounded self-adjoint operators, spectral measures and the usual ZFC set theory with classical first-order logic in the background. That formalism is a first-order, non-modal language whose intended models are the specific Hilbert space models of a given system and their Stone-von Neumann representations. It contains no primitive modal operator and no built-in notion of a domain of possible worlds.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a theorem of modal predicate logic, in the standard presentation S5 with an axiom of necessary existence for positive properties. Its proof is a proof in Kripke semantics for S5 and it is essentially a metatheoretic argument about essential properties and necessity. To even state the axioms one needs a bona fide modal language with the □ operator and a semantics that interprets □ as truth in all accessible worlds.

No such operator is definable within the customary quantum-mechanical formalism itself. Projection operators, POVMs and the usual algebraic structures are used to represent physical properties as yes/no questions in one fixed world, i.e. in one Hilbert space, and they do not provide a well-founded Kripke frame of metaphysically distinct possible worlds with the S5 accessibility relation. Any attempt to encode a possible worlds structure would require an extra-metatheoretic extension of the Hilbert space language – essentially importing classical modal logic on top of the physical mathematics – which is not part of the customary setting of quantum mechanics.

Hence, within the usual Hilbert-space, operator-algebraic mathematics used for quantum theory, the modal axioms needed for Gödel’s god-like entity are not expressible, let alone provable. The existence claim remains outside the formal system used for quantum mechanics.

4.text:
In the physics literature the mathematics which is actually used for quantum
mechanics is classical first order mathematics. Up to the usual background
set theory it is

* ZFC + the usual analysis over $\mathbb C$,
* complete inner product spaces, bounded/unbounded self-adjoint
operators, spectral theory etc.,

i.e. the ordinary classical, non-modal, first order apparatus in which
existence means set theoretic existence. The Born rule, the spectral
theorem and so on are theorems of that apparatus. There is no modal
operator $\Box,\Diamond$ and no primitive notion of `positive property',
`essence', `necessary existence' etc. in the Hilbert space formalism.

Gödel's ontological argument is a theorem of a modal logic, essentially
the modal system S5 with the additional axiom schema

P1 $P(x)\rightarrow \Box \forall x\,[P(x)\rightarrow P(x)]$, 
P2 $P(x)\rightarrow P(\neg P(x))$ is impossible,
P3 $\Box\exists x\,P(x)\rightarrow P(x)$ is positive,
etc.

and the definition

God-like $=$ $\forall P\,[{\rm Positive}(P)\rightarrow P(x)]$.

Once those axioms are taken as given the S5 derivation

$ \Box\exists x{\rm Godlike}(x)\vdash \exists x{\rm Godlike}(x) $

goes through. The derivation is a formal derivation in the metalanguage
of ZFC, and it can of course be written down in the same set-theoretic
language in which a Hilbert space is defined. That is a purely syntactic
embedding. It is not a theorem of the ordinary mathematical apparatus of
quantum mechanics.

In the usual first order/classical mathematics the axioms about
positivity, about the closure of positive properties under entailment and
about necessary existence are not mathematical theorems of ZFC + analysis;
they are metaphysical postulates. Hence the existence of a Gödel god-like
being is not provable from the customary Hilbert-space/operator
mathematics of quantum mechanics alone. At best it is a conditional
provability: assuming the controversial S5 positivity axioms, the
existence of a necessary maximally great being follows in the background
set theory. Without those extra-modal, essentially theological, premises
the formalism of quantum mechanics gives you no statement about a
God-like entity at all. That is the well known status of Gödel's ontological
proof.

6.text:
The mathematics in which ordinary quantum mechanics is written is the ordinary
mathematics of the formalist tradition, ZF(C) first order logic with
Hilbert spaces, C*-algebras etc. built in it. In that background you can
indeed formalise Gödel’s ontological argument as a derivation in a
modal propositional system, essentially S5 with a predicate $P$ for
positive property.

Let

* $P(x)$ be $x$ has only positive properties,
* $G(x)$ be $x$ is God-like,
* $\Box$ be metaphysical necessity.

The Gödel axioms are

1. $\Box P(x)\rightarrow P(x)$,
2. $P(x)\rightarrow \Box P(x)$,
3. $P(x)\rightarrow P(\Box x)$,
4. $P(x)\land P(y)\rightarrow P(x\land y)$,
5. $P(\exists y R(x,y))\rightarrow \exists y\,P(R(x,y))$,
6. $P(E)$ where $E(x)$ is “$x$ exists”,
and $G(x)\equiv\forall P\big(P(x)\rightarrow P(x)\big)$.

From these in S5 you get $\Box\exists x\,G(x)$ and hence
$\exists x\,G(x)$.  The derivation is a purely formal one, and it can
be carried out in the set theory in which a separable complex Hilbert
space, self-adjoint operators and the usual spectral calculus live.
That is the only sense in which the proof can be “done” in the
customary QM mathematics.

What the formalisation does not give you is a mathematical theorem of
ZFC + classical logic.  The axioms 1–6 are not mathematical axioms.
The notion of “positive”, of “existence as a positive property” and
of the modal $\Box$ are metaphysical, not set theoretic.  The proof is
conditional

$A_{\rm Pos}\vdash_{\rm S5}\exists x\,G(x) $

and the premises $A_{\rm Pos}$ are not derivable in, and are in fact
independent of, the formal system that underlies quantum mechanics.
In particular the derivation uses the classical Boolean distributive
lattice of properties on which ordinary first order logic rests.  If
the logic is replaced by the orthomodular quantum logic that is
sometimes associated with the physics, distributivity is lost and the
usual propositional steps of Gödel’s derivation break down.  So in
the strict mathematical sense there is no unconditional theorem of the
mathematics of quantum mechanics whose content is “a necessarily
existent God-like entity exists”.  At best you obtain a conditional
validity: if the metaphysical positivity axioms are accepted as true,
S5 yields the existence of a being with all positive properties.
That is exactly Gödel’s own view, and it is not a mathematical proof
of existence in the ordinary Hilbert-space sense.

8.text:
The mathematics that is actually used to do quantum mechanics is the
ordinary classical mathematics of Hilbert spaces, operators, spectral
theory, C*-algebras etc. It is formalised in the ordinary set theoretic
meta-theory ZFC + classical first order logic which is also the
meta-theory in which the usual mathematics of physics is carried out.

Godel's ontological argument is a derivation in modal logic S5 from a
small set of essentially metaphysical axioms about `positive' properties,
essence and existence being positive. It is a purely syntactic
derivation. In that formal sense it can be embedded in the same classical
first order meta-theory which underlies the Hilbert space formalism, so
there is no formal syntactic obstacle to writing the derivation down in
the same language in which you write down the Schrödinger equation.

That is all the embedding amounts to. The axioms

*  P is positive iff  ¬P is not positive,
*  If P is positive and P→Q then Q is positive,
*  Existence is positive,
*  Necessity of positive properties, etc.

and the modal machinery of S5 are not part of the empirical content of
quantum theory, nor are they definable in terms of self adjoint
operators, projection lattices or states on a Hilbert space. The
mathematical apparatus of quantum mechanics gives you no criterion for
what counts as a positive property, for essence, for maximal greatness,
or for the modal accessibility relation that is required for the
argument to go through. 

In a scientifically meaningful sense the argument therefore does not
follow from, and is not justified by, the mathematics used for quantum
mechanics. Formally you can write the modal proof down in the classical
background that is also used for physics, but you have not gained any
physical or empirical warrant for the existence of a maximally great
being. The proof is a formal exercise in classical modal logic, not a
theorem of quantum theory.

and under the usual S5 axioms one indeed derives □∃x Gx. That is to say the
statement “a being which has every positive property necessarily exists’’ is a
theorem of the modal theory once the five positivity axioms are granted.

The derivation is therefore not a matter of physics at all. It is a purely
syntactic consequence of the chosen axioms. What it gives you is not a physical
existence claim but the formal consistency statement

Consistent(S5+Gödel axioms) → ⊢ □∃x Gx

in the same set-theoretic metatheory in which H is defined. In particular it
gives no warrant that a “God-like’’ entity exists in the external world, and the
quantum mechanical formalism, which is the same classical mathematics plus the
non-commutative lattice of closed subspaces of H, adds no new ontological
power. The axioms about what counts as positive and about the modal
interaction of necessity and implication are not part of the physical theory and
are notoriously contentious.

In the usual philosophical sense this is therefore not a proof of existence at
all. Moreover, on the usual reading the existence of a necessarily existent
being is essentially the statement of the consistency of the system in which it
is formulated. By Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem a sufficiently strong,
recursively axiomatizable system such as the one that can talk about H and about
arithmetic cannot prove its own consistency internally, so there is no internal
non-conditional proof of a necessarily existent being within the customary
mathematical setting of quantum mechanics. The at best formal derivability of
Gödel’s argument is a logical curiosity, not a physical proof.

In the mathematics that is actually used when one does ordinary quantum
mechanics the Hilbert space ${\cal H}$ over ${\mathbf C}$, the $C^{*}$–algebra
of observables, the spectral theory etc., is interpreted in the ordinary
classical metatheory ZFC + classical first order logic + the usual analysis
of the real and complex numbers.  In that metatheory you can formalise
first order modal logic $S5$, you can formalise the set of properties
$P$ and the usual Gödel axioms

* $P$ is closed under entailment,
* if $P\in P$ then $\neg P\notin P$,
* $\Phi\in P\;\to\;\Box\Phi\in P$,
* $\exists x\,\Phi(x)\in P$,

together with the conventional S5 axioms for $\Box$ and you can then
formalise Gödel’s argument

$\exists x\,\Phi(x)\in P$, $\Phi\in P\Rightarrow\Box\Phi\in P$ etc. $\;\vdash\;
\Box\exists x\,G(x)$, and in $S5$

$\Box\exists x\,G(x)\to\exists x\,\Box G(x)$,

so that in the formal system you get the familiar conditional theorem

$G(x)\equiv \forall\Phi\,[\Phi\in P\leftrightarrow\Phi(x)]$ implies
$\Box\exists x\,G(x)$ and hence $\exists x\,\Box G(x)$.

In other words the ontological argument is a purely syntactic theorem of
the classical modal logic in which functional analysis is written down.
It is provable in the same ZFC + PA + analysis that underlies the
Hilbert-space formalism, and in that purely formal sense it is “available’’
to the quantum mechanic.  It is of course a conditional derivability: it
is a theorem relative to the highly contentious metaphysical axioms about
positivity, about the closure of $P$ under $\Box$, and about the
identification of $G(x)$ with the being that has all positive properties.
Changing the background mathematics to the usual complex Hilbert space
adds no new ontological content and does not make the axioms true in the
physical world.

If the quantum content is taken seriously, the propositions of ordinary
quantum mechanics are generally taken to form an orthomodular rather than
a Boolean lattice.  Classical distributivity and the classical $S5$ modal
scheme used by Gödel are not validated by that quantum logical structure,
so the Gödel argument does not survive a literal quantum-logical
interpretation of necessity and of conjunction/disjunction of properties.
In the substantive, physically meaningful sense there is therefore no new
proof of the existence of a Gödel god-like being supplied by the
formalism of quantum mechanics; at best you can write the classical
modal proof down inside the classical mathematics that is the ordinary
metatheory of Hilbert spaces.  That formal derivability is not a physical
or metaphysical proof of the existence of God.

No. 

The mathematics that is actually customarily used for quantum mechanics is the ordinary classical formalism of functional analysis: separable complex Hilbert spaces, bounded self-adjoint operators, spectral measures and the usual ZFC set theory with classical first-order logic in the background. That formalism is a first-order, non-modal language whose intended models are the specific Hilbert space models of a given system and their Stone-von Neumann representations. It contains no primitive modal operator and no built-in notion of a domain of possible worlds.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a theorem of modal predicate logic, in the standard presentation S5 with an axiom of necessary existence for positive properties. Its proof is a proof in Kripke semantics for S5 and it is essentially a metatheoretic argument about essential properties and necessity. To even state the axioms one needs a bona fide modal language with the □ operator and a semantics that interprets □ as truth in all accessible worlds.

No such operator is definable within the customary quantum-mechanical formalism itself. Projection operators, POVMs and the usual algebraic structures are used to represent physical properties as yes/no questions in one fixed world, i.e. in one Hilbert space, and they do not provide a well-founded Kripke frame of metaphysically distinct possible worlds with the S5 accessibility relation. Any attempt to encode a possible worlds structure would require an extra-metatheoretic extension of the Hilbert space language – essentially importing classical modal logic on top of the physical mathematics – which is not part of the customary setting of quantum mechanics.

Hence, within the usual Hilbert-space, operator-algebraic mathematics used for quantum theory, the modal axioms needed for Gödel’s god-like entity are not expressible, let alone provable. The existence claim remains outside the formal system used for quantum mechanics.

In the physics literature the mathematics which is actually used for quantum
mechanics is classical first order mathematics. Up to the usual background
set theory it is

* ZFC + the usual analysis over $\mathbb C$,
* complete inner product spaces, bounded/unbounded self-adjoint
operators, spectral theory etc.,

i.e. the ordinary classical, non-modal, first order apparatus in which
existence means set theoretic existence. The Born rule, the spectral
theorem and so on are theorems of that apparatus. There is no modal
operator $\Box,\Diamond$ and no primitive notion of `positive property',
`essence', `necessary existence' etc. in the Hilbert space formalism.

Gödel's ontological argument is a theorem of a modal logic, essentially
the modal system S5 with the additional axiom schema

P1 $P(x)\rightarrow \Box \forall x\,[P(x)\rightarrow P(x)]$, 
P2 $P(x)\rightarrow P(\neg P(x))$ is impossible,
P3 $\Box\exists x\,P(x)\rightarrow P(x)$ is positive,
etc.

and the definition

God-like $=$ $\forall P\,[{\rm Positive}(P)\rightarrow P(x)]$.

Once those axioms are taken as given the S5 derivation

$ \Box\exists x{\rm Godlike}(x)\vdash \exists x{\rm Godlike}(x) $

goes through. The derivation is a formal derivation in the metalanguage
of ZFC, and it can of course be written down in the same set-theoretic
language in which a Hilbert space is defined. That is a purely syntactic
embedding. It is not a theorem of the ordinary mathematical apparatus of
quantum mechanics.

In the usual first order/classical mathematics the axioms about
positivity, about the closure of positive properties under entailment and
about necessary existence are not mathematical theorems of ZFC + analysis;
they are metaphysical postulates. Hence the existence of a Gödel god-like
being is not provable from the customary Hilbert-space/operator
mathematics of quantum mechanics alone. At best it is a conditional
provability: assuming the controversial S5 positivity axioms, the
existence of a necessary maximally great being follows in the background
set theory. Without those extra-modal, essentially theological, premises
the formalism of quantum mechanics gives you no statement about a
God-like entity at all. That is the well known status of Gödel's ontological
proof.

The mathematics in which ordinary quantum mechanics is written is the ordinary
mathematics of the formalist tradition, ZF(C) first order logic with
Hilbert spaces, C*-algebras etc. built in it. In that background you can
indeed formalise Gödel’s ontological argument as a derivation in a
modal propositional system, essentially S5 with a predicate $P$ for
positive property.

Let

* $P(x)$ be $x$ has only positive properties,
* $G(x)$ be $x$ is God-like,
* $\Box$ be metaphysical necessity.

The Gödel axioms are

1. $\Box P(x)\rightarrow P(x)$,
2. $P(x)\rightarrow \Box P(x)$,
3. $P(x)\rightarrow P(\Box x)$,
4. $P(x)\land P(y)\rightarrow P(x\land y)$,
5. $P(\exists y R(x,y))\rightarrow \exists y\,P(R(x,y))$,
6. $P(E)$ where $E(x)$ is “$x$ exists”,
and $G(x)\equiv\forall P\big(P(x)\rightarrow P(x)\big)$.

From these in S5 you get $\Box\exists x\,G(x)$ and hence
$\exists x\,G(x)$.  The derivation is a purely formal one, and it can
be carried out in the set theory in which a separable complex Hilbert
space, self-adjoint operators and the usual spectral calculus live.
That is the only sense in which the proof can be “done” in the
customary QM mathematics.

What the formalisation does not give you is a mathematical theorem of
ZFC + classical logic.  The axioms 1–6 are not mathematical axioms.
The notion of “positive”, of “existence as a positive property” and
of the modal $\Box$ are metaphysical, not set theoretic.  The proof is
conditional

$A_{\rm Pos}\vdash_{\rm S5}\exists x\,G(x) $

and the premises $A_{\rm Pos}$ are not derivable in, and are in fact
independent of, the formal system that underlies quantum mechanics.
In particular the derivation uses the classical Boolean distributive
lattice of properties on which ordinary first order logic rests.  If
the logic is replaced by the orthomodular quantum logic that is
sometimes associated with the physics, distributivity is lost and the
usual propositional steps of Gödel’s derivation break down.  So in
the strict mathematical sense there is no unconditional theorem of the
mathematics of quantum mechanics whose content is “a necessarily
existent God-like entity exists”.  At best you obtain a conditional
validity: if the metaphysical positivity axioms are accepted as true,
S5 yields the existence of a being with all positive properties.
That is exactly Gödel’s own view, and it is not a mathematical proof
of existence in the ordinary Hilbert-space sense.
public_text.8:
The mathematics that is actually used to do quantum mechanics is the
ordinary classical mathematics of Hilbert spaces, operators, spectral
theory, C*-algebras etc. It is formalised in the ordinary set theoretic
meta-theory ZFC + classical first order logic which is also the
meta-theory in which the usual mathematics of physics is carried out.

Godel's ontological argument is a derivation in modal logic S5 from a
small set of essentially metaphysical axioms about `positive' properties,
essence and existence being positive. It is a purely syntactic
derivation. In that formal sense it can be embedded in the same classical
first order meta-theory which underlies the Hilbert space formalism, so
there is no formal syntactic obstacle to writing the derivation down in
the same language in which you write down the Schrödinger equation.

That is all the embedding amounts to. The axioms

*  P is positive iff  ¬P is not positive,
*  If P is positive and P→Q then Q is positive,
*  Existence is positive,
*  Necessity of positive properties, etc.

and the modal machinery of S5 are not part of the empirical content of
quantum theory, nor are they definable in terms of self adjoint
operators, projection lattices or states on a Hilbert space. The
mathematical apparatus of quantum mechanics gives you no criterion for
what counts as a positive property, for essence, for maximal greatness,
or for the modal accessibility relation that is required for the
argument to go through. 

In a scientifically meaningful sense the argument therefore does not
follow from, and is not justified by, the mathematics used for quantum
mechanics. Formally you can write the modal proof down in the classical
background that is also used for physics, but you have not gained any
physical or empirical warrant for the existence of a maximally great
being. The proof is a formal exercise in classical modal logic, not a
theorem of quantum theory.

Gödel's ontological argument is a modal argument: S5 with □ and a predicate Positive(P) with axioms P1–P5, e.g. necessity of positivity, closure under entailment, existence is positive, etc., and G(x) := ∧_{P positive} P(x). In S5+those axioms one gets ⊢ □∃x Gx → ∃x Gx and hence the conditional theorem ⊢ ∃x Gx.

Formal embeddability:
* The metatheory that underlies the Hilbert-space formalism, ZFC + classical analysis, can interpret first-order logic, classical second-order logic and S5. Non-physical / non-internal:
* The customary QM formalism has no primitive modal operator □ and no built-in Kripke frame of possible worlds. Projection operators/POVMs represent yes/no questions in one fixed world/Hilbert space. 4.text:
The mathematics that is actually used to state, compute and verify quantum-mechanical predictions is classical mathematics.  Non-relativistic QM is done in ZFC + analysis: a separable complex Hilbert space H, B(H), self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, states, the Born rule, etc.  That background is first-order classical, non-modal, with existence meaning set-theoretic existence in the usual models.

Gödel’s argument is a theorem of modal predicate logic.  In the usual rendering it is S5 + a positivity predicate P with

* P1- P5 the closure/necessity/existence axioms,
* Gx := ∧_{P} P x, i.e. x has every positive property,

and the S5 bridge principles □P → P, P → □P, etc.  The derivation

□∃x Gx ⊢ ∃x Gx

is a purely syntactic derivation in classical modal logic.

That syntactic derivation can be coded in the same metatheory in which H is coded. ZFC can interpret first-order logic, second-order arithmetic and the usual Kripke semantics for S5, so the axioms P1-P5 and the definition of G can be formalised in the set-theoretic language used for functional analysis, and the formal derivation can be written down verbatim in the classical metalanguage. In that purely formal, conditional sense

S5 + P1–P5 ⊢ □∃x Gx and hence ⊢ ∃x Gx

is a theorem of the classical background shared by QM.

It is not a theorem of quantum mechanics. The positivity axioms, the necessity operator □, the notion of essence and the S5 accessibility relation are not definable in terms of vectors, projections, observables or states. They are metaphysical postulates about properties of beings, not theorems of spectral theory or C*–algebra theory, and they have no operational content in the Born rule. Physically meaningful propositions in the standard formalism are elements of the orthomodular lattice P(H) of closed subspaces, quantum logic, not a classical Boolean modal algebra. The classical distributive steps and the S5 modal schemata Gödel uses are not validated by that orthomodular structure, and the modal operator has no internal interpretation in the Hilbert-space language.

Hence there is no unconditional, physically meaningful proof of a Gödel god-like entity from the customary quantum-mechanical formalism. At best one obtains a conditional syntactic derivability in the classical ZFC metatheory that underlies both QM and ordinary mathematics. That formal derivability gives no empirical warrant and by Gödel’s second incompleteness the necessity of existence is essentially a consistency statement the system cannot prove internally. The proof is a formal exercise in classical modal logic, not a theorem of quantum theory.

1.text:
In the customary mathematics in which non-relativistic and relativistic
quantum mechanics is actually written down there is no internal proof.

The customary setting is ZFC + analysis, complex separable / non-separable
Hilbert spaces, self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, C*-algebras,
first-order classical logic in the background.  That is a non-modal,
first-order language whose intended models are a fixed Hilbert space and
its operators.  It contains no primitive $\Box,\Diamond$, no Kripke frame,
no primitive notion of ‘positive property’, ‘essence’ or ‘necessary
existence’, and the physically meaningful propositional structure is the
orthomodular lattice $P(H)$ of projections, not a classical Boolean modal
algebra.

Gödel’s derivation is a theorem of S5 predicate logic plus the five
metaphysical positivity axioms P1–P5 and the definition
$G(x)\equiv \bigwedge_{P}{\rm Positive}(P)\to P(x)$.  In the classical
metatheory ZFC in which Hilbert space theory is formalised one can of
course code an S5 Kripke semantics, introduce a predicate Positive and
write down the derivation

$\Box\Diamond\exists x Gx\to \exists x Gx$,

and under the bridge principles $\Box\exists x Gx\leftrightarrow\exists x
\Box Gx$ etc. obtain the familiar conditional
$S5+P1\!-\!P5\vdash \exists x Gx$.
That is a purely syntactic embedding. The five positivity axioms,
the S5 necessity operator and the notion of a maximally great being are
not theorems of functional analysis, spectral theory or C*-algebra theory,
and they have no operational meaning in the Hilbert-space formalism.
The derivation uses classical distributivity and the S5 schemata which are
not validated by the orthomodular quantum logic that is native to the
formalism.

Hence there is no theorem of the mathematics of quantum mechanics, and
no physically meaningful consequence of quantum mechanics, whose content is
the existence of a Gödel god-like entity.  At best one obtains a
conditional formal derivability in the classical set-theoretic
metatheory that is used to express the theory.  That is the same vacuous
formal status the argument has in PA or in any classical metatheory, and
it gives no physical or metaphysical warrant for the existence claim.
In the strict internal sense required of a proof from quantum mechanics the
answer is no. ∎

8.text:
In the customary mathematics of quantum mechanics the Hilbert space, operator and C*-algebraic formalism is written in classical first order mathematics, essentially ZFC + analysis over C. That meta-theory is classical, non-modal and first order.

That meta-theory is expressive enough to code first order modal logic S5 and to code the predicate Positive(P) and the definition
G(x) := ∧_{P positive} P(x). 
Once the five Gödelian positivity axioms and the S5 bridge principles are taken as extra premises, the derivation

□∃x Gx → ∃x Gx

and hence the conditional theorem ⊢ ∃x Gx

can be written down in the same set-theoretic language in which the spectral theorem, Stone–von Neumann etc. are written. In the purely syntactic sense the ontological argument is formally embeddable in the classical metatheory that underlies QM, just as it is embeddable in PA.

That is not a theorem of quantum mechanics. The Hilbert space formalism has no primitive □ and no built-in Kripke frame of metaphysically distinct possible worlds. Projection operators, POVMs and states represent yes/no questions in one fixed world. The positivity axioms, essence, necessary existence are metaphysical postulates about a class of properties. They are not definable in terms of vectors, observables or spectra and they have no operational content in QM.

Physically the propositions of the theory are usually read on the orthomodular lattice P(H) of closed subspaces. Classical distributivity and the S5 modal schemata on which Gödel’s derivation is presented fail on that lattice, so the derivation does not survive a literal quantum-logical interpretation. In particular the axioms P1–P5 are not theorems of analysis, spectral theory, C*-algebra theory or quantum logic.

Hence there is no unconditional, physically meaningful proof of a Gödel god-like entity from the customary Hilbert-space mathematics of quantum mechanics. At best one obtains a conditional formal derivability in the classical set-theoretic metatheory that one uses to formalise QM, conditional on highly contentious metaphysical positivity axioms which the physical theory neither supplies nor justifies. Formal embeddability ≠ internal proof.

2.text:
In the customary mathematical language in which non-relativistic and relativistic quantum mechanics is written the theory is formalised in ZFC + classical analysis. That is a classical first-order, non-modal language:

* a complex separable Hilbert space H,
* B(H), self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, C*-algebras,
* the usual first-order classical logic of the metatheory.

In that language existence is set theoretic existence, and there is no primitive modal operator □, ◇, no primitive notion of possible world, of essence, of “positive property”, and no built-in Kripke frame with S5 accessibility. Physical propositions are represented operationally by projections, states and observables in one fixed Hilbert space; the native propositional calculus of the formalism is classical in the meta-theory and, if taken in the Birkhoff-von Neumann sense, orthomodular in the object theory.

Gödel’s argument is a theorem of modal predicate logic S5 plus the metaphysical positivity axioms

P1–P5,  Existence is positive,  P → □ P, etc.,

and the definition G(x) ≡ ∧_{P positive} P(x). The derivation

⊢_{S5} □ ◇ ∃x Gx → ∃x Gx

and with the bridge principles

⊢ ∃x Gx ,  ⊢ □ ∃x Gx

is a purely syntactic derivation of classical modal logic.

Hence in the metatheory ZFC+analysis in which H, B(H) and the spectral theorem are defined one can code the syntax of S5, define a predicate “positive”, and transcribe Gödel’s derivation verbatim. In that purely syntactic sense the argument can be written down in the same classical mathematics that underlies quantum mechanics. 

That is all the embedding amounts to. The positivity axioms, the S5 necessity operator, the notion of a property being necessarily positive, and the identification of existence with a positive property are not theorems of analysis, of spectral theory, of C*-algebra theory, nor are they definable in terms of vectors, projections or observables. They are substantive metaphysical postulates. The derivation is therefore the conditional

A_Pos + S5 ⊢ ∃x Gx

in the background set theory, not an unconditional theorem of the physical theory. 

In particular the proof uses the ordinary classical distributive propositional calculus on which S5 is presented. If the logic of properties is taken literally as the orthomodular lattice P(H) of quantum propositions, distributivity fails and the S5 steps do not survive a literal quantum-logical interpretation of conjunction, disjunction and necessity.

So there is no internal proof of a necessarily existent maximally positive being as a theorem of the Hilbert-space/operator-algebraic formalism of quantum mechanics, and no physical or empirical warrant for the positivity axioms is supplied by the formalism. The argument is formally transcribable in the classical metatheory used for QM, but it remains a conditional formal exercise, not a physical proof of existence.

5.text:
In the customary mathematics that is actually used to state, compute and verify quantum mechanical predictions the proof is not available internally.

The working mathematics of non-relativistic and relativistic quantum theory is

* ZFC + classical first order logic + analysis,
* separable / non-separable complex Hilbert spaces, bounded and unbounded self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, C*-algebras.

That is a non-modal first order apparatus. Its intended models are one fixed Hilbert space and its representations. The language contains no primitive modal operator □, no Kripke frame of possible worlds, no predicate Positive(P) and no notion of essence or necessary existence. Projection operators, POVMs, states and the orthomodular lattice P(H) represent properties as yes/no questions in one world.

Gödel's ontological argument is a theorem of S5 modal predicate logic from the axioms

P1 □[Positive(P)→¬Positive(¬P)],
P2 Positive(P)→Positive(□P),
P3 Positive(P) → □Positive(P),
P4 Positive(P) ∧ (P→Q) → Positive(Q),
P5 Positive(∃x),
G(x) ≡ ∀P[Positive(P)→P(x)],

and the S5 bridge principles □∃xGx → ∃x□Gx etc. The derivation
⊢_{S5+P1–P5} □∃xGx and hence ∃xGx
is a purely syntactic conditional theorem of classical modal logic.

That derivation can, trivially, be transcribed in the classical set-theoretic meta-theory in which the Hilbert space formalism is written down. ZFC can interpret first order logic, second order logic and S5, so the axioms and the derivation can be written as sentences of the same background theory that defines the spectral theorem, Stone–von Neumann etc. In that purely formal sense the argument is available in the same metatheory.

It is not a theorem of quantum mechanics. The positivity axioms, the S5 necessity operator, essence and necessary existence are metaphysical postulates. They are not definable in terms of vectors, projections, observables or states, nor are they empirically testable. In particular the physical propositional structure that is native to QM in the Birkhoff–von Neumann reading is the orthomodular lattice P(H), not the Boolean classical propositional calculus on which the S5 schemata and the usual distributive steps of the Gödel proof rest. The modal axioms are therefore not expressible, let alone provable, in the customary Hilbert-space / operator-algebraic language.

Hence there is no unconditional proof of a Gödel god-like entity from the mathematics actually used for quantum mechanics. At best one gets the conditional formal derivability

A_Pos ⊢_{S5} ∃xGx

in the classical metatheory that underlies the mathematics of QM. That is a logical curiosity, not a physical or mathematical proof of existence.

positivity axioms, and those axioms are neither theorems nor empirically
testable consequences of analysis, spectral theory, $C^{*}$-algebra theory or
quantum logic.  In the physically meaningful, operational sense there is no
internal proof of a real god-like maximally positive entity from the Hilbert

The mathematics that is actually used to formulate and compute with quantum mechanics is classical first-order mathematics. * $P(\varphi)\rightarrow \Box P(\varphi)$,

* $P(E)$ where $E$ is existence,
* $G(x)\equiv\forall\Phi[P(\Phi)\rightarrow \Phi(x)]$,

is a conditional theorem of the classical metatheory that underlies QM, exactly as it is a theorem of PA. That is all the transcription amounts to.

They have no operational meaning in terms of states, observables or spectra. The axioms P1–P5 are metaphysical stipulations; they are not theorems of functional analysis, spectral theory, $C^{*}$-algebra theory or of the orthomodular quantum logic that is physically meaningful inside the theory. In particular the classical distributive Boolean calculus on which the S5 derivation is usually presented is not validated by $P(H)$.

Hence in the physically meaningful, internal sense there is no proof of a Gödel god-like entity from the customary mathematics of quantum mechanics. At best one obtains a conditional formal validity in the classical set-theoretic metatheory that one uses to write down QM, which is a logical curiosity and not a physical or empirical proof of existence.

and the S5 bridge principles □P → P, P → □P, etc.  The derivation

□∃x Gx ⊢ ∃x Gx

is a purely syntactic derivation in classical modal logic.

That syntactic derivation can be coded in the same metatheory in which H is coded. ZFC can interpret first-order logic, second-order arithmetic and the usual Kripke semantics for S5, so the axioms P1-P5 and the definition of G can be formalised in the set-theoretic language used for functional analysis, and the formal derivation can be written down verbatim in the classical metalanguage. In that purely formal, conditional sense

S5 + P1–P5 ⊢ □∃x Gx and hence ⊢ ∃x Gx

is a theorem of the classical background shared by QM.

It is not a theorem of quantum mechanics. The positivity axioms, the necessity operator □, the notion of essence and the S5 accessibility relation are not definable in terms of vectors, projections, observables or states. They are metaphysical postulates about properties of beings, not theorems of spectral theory or C*–algebra theory, and they have no operational content in the Born rule. Physically meaningful propositions in the standard formalism are elements of the orthomodular lattice P(H) of closed subspaces, quantum logic, not a classical Boolean modal algebra. The classical distributive steps and the S5 modal schemata Gödel uses are not validated by that orthomodular structure, and the modal operator has no internal interpretation in the Hilbert-space language.

Hence there is no unconditional, physically meaningful proof of a Gödel god-like entity from the customary quantum-mechanical formalism. At best one obtains a conditional syntactic derivability in the classical ZFC metatheory that underlies both QM and ordinary mathematics. That formal derivability gives no empirical warrant and by Gödel’s second incompleteness the necessity of existence is essentially a consistency statement the system cannot prove internally. The proof is a formal exercise in classical modal logic, not a theorem of quantum theory.

reflection_text.2:

Object-language is non-modal, first-order, existence = set-theoretic existence in a fixed Hilbert-space model. Physically meaningful propositional structure is read as the orthomodular lattice P(H) of closed subspaces / projections, quantum logic, not a Boolean S5 modal algebra.

Gödel’s argument = S5 predicate logic + positivity predicate P with P1–P5 and G(x) := ∧_{P positive} P(x). Derivation ⊢_{S5+P} □∃xGx → ∃xGx and with bridge principles ⊢ ∃xGx, ⊢ □∃xGx.

Formal embeddability consensus from both rounds: ZFC+analysis can interpret first-order logic, second-order arithmetic and set-theoretic Kripke semantics for S5. Hence the five positivity axioms, the definition of G, the S5 schemata and the whole derivation can be transcribed as sentences of the same classical metatheory in which H, spectral theorem, Stone–von Neumann etc. are defined. In that purely syntactic/metatheoretic sense the proof is writable down, and the conditional theorem S5+P1–P5 ⊢ ∃xGx is a theorem of the classical background shared by QM. This is the formalist camp 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9.

Physical/internal non-provability consensus: The customary QM formalism has no primitive □,◇, no Kripke frame of metaphysically distinct possible worlds, no primitive notion of positive property/essence/necessary existence. Projection operators, POVMs, states represent yes/no questions in one fixed world. The positivity axioms, necessity of positive properties, existence as positive, etc. are metaphysical postulates, not theorems of analysis, spectral theory, C*-algebra theory, nor definable in terms of vectors, projections, observables or spectra. They have no operational meaning or empirical testability.

Orthomodular objection: If propositions are taken literally as P(H), classical distributivity and the Boolean S5 modal schemata on which Gödel’s derivation is presented fail. The argument does not survive a literal quantum-logical interpretation of conjunction/disjunction/necessity.

Common point: Derivation is conditional on highly contentious S5 positivity axioms. At best one gets Consistent(S5+Gödel axioms) → ⊢ □∃xGx in the background set theory. By Gödel’s second incompleteness, necessary existence is essentially a consistency statement the system cannot prove internally.

Split on wording of “possible”: 
* Formalist reading: yes, you can transcribe the proof in the classical metatheory used for QM, conditional on the axioms, and that is the usual way the argument is said to be formally valid.
* Strict internal reading: no, the modal apparatus is extra-metatheoretic; within the Hilbert-space/operator-algebraic first-order language actually used to state, compute and verify predictions the modal operator and axioms are not expressible, let alone provable.

Orthomodular quantum-logic objection shows the argument would break down if necessity/properties were identified with quantum propositions. Unresolved for final answer is whether the question intends metatheoretic formal derivability or internal provability from physics; literature usually treats metatheory as part of setting, making formal derivability trivial, substantive claim being no physical proof.

In the mathematics that is actually used to state and compute quantum mechanics there is no
internal proof.

The working formalism is classical first-order mathematics: ZFC + analysis, a complex
Hilbert space H, B(H) or a C*-algebra of observables, self-adjoint operators, spectral
measures, states, Born rule, etc.  Existence in that language is set-theoretic
existence in a fixed model. The language is non-modal: there is no primitive
$\Box,\Diamond$, no Kripke frame of metaphysically distinct possible worlds, no
primitive notion of positive property, essence or necessary existence. Physically
meaningful propositions are represented by projections/POVMs and, in the
Birkhoff-von Neumann reading, by the orthomodular lattice $P(H)$, not by a Boolean
S5 modal algebra.

Gödel’s argument is a theorem of modal predicate logic S5 plus the five
metaphysical positivity axioms P1–P5 and

$G(x)\equiv\bigwedge_{P\;{\rm positive}}P(x)$

with the S5 bridge principles
$\Box\Diamond\exists x Gx\to\exists x Gx$, 
$\Box\exists x Gx\to\exists x\Box Gx$, etc.
The derivation

$S5+P1\!-\!P5\vdash\Box\exists x Gx$ and hence $\vdash\exists x Gx$

uses classical distributivity and the S5 schemata. It is a conditional syntactic
theorem of classical modal logic.

ZFC+analysis in which $H$, $B(H)$ and the spectral theorem are defined can of
course code first order logic, second order logic and a set-theoretic Kripke
semantics for S5. Hence in the classical metatheory that underlies the
formalisation of QM the axioms P1–P5, the predicate Positive and the usual S5
derivation can be transcribed verbatim. In that purely formal, metatheoretic
sense the ontological argument is embeddable in the same background set theory
that is used to write down QM, exactly as it is embeddable in PA.

That is formal embeddability, not internal provability. The positivity axioms,
the S5 necessity operator, the notion of essence and necessary existence are
metaphysical postulates. They are not theorems of functional analysis, spectral
theory, C*-algebra theory or quantum logic, and they have no operational meaning
in terms of vectors, observables, spectra or Born probabilities. In particular
the classical Boolean distributive propositional calculus on which the S5
derivation rests is not validated by the orthomodular lattice $P(H)$ that is
native to the physical content of the theory, and $\Box$ has no interpretation in
the Hilbert-space/operator-algebraic language.

Hence there is no unconditional, physically meaningful theorem of the
customary Hilbert-space / operator-algebraic mathematics of quantum mechanics
whose content is the existence of a necessarily existent maximally positive
being. At best one obtains the conditional formal derivability

$A_{\rm Pos}+S5 \vdash \exists x Gx$

in the classical set-theoretic metatheory used to formalise QM. That gives no
physical or empirical warrant and by Gödel’s second incompleteness the
necessity of existence is essentially a consistency statement the system cannot
prove internally. In the strict internal, operational sense required of a proof
from quantum mechanics the answer is no.

Physically meaningful propositions are projections/POVMs, and in the Birkhoff-von Neumann reading the native propositional structure is the orthomodular lattice P(H), not Boolean S5. The working language is non-modal: no primitive □/◇, no Kripke frame of metaphysically distinct worlds, no primitive predicate Positive, essence or necessary existence. Existence in that formalism is set-theoretic existence in a fixed model.

Gödel’s ontological argument is an S5 modal predicate derivation from P1–P5 and G := λx. ∧_{P positive} P x, using classical distributivity and S5 bridge principles □∃x Gx ↔ ∃x □Gx etc. All colleagues in round 2 agree the derivation is a conditional syntactic theorem S5+P1–P5 ⊢ □∃x Gx and hence ⊢ ∃x Gx, and uses no Hilbert-space structure.

ZFC+analysis can interpret first-order logic, second-order arithmetic and a set-theoretic Kripke semantics for S5. Hence in the classical set-theoretic metatheory that underlies the definition of H, the spectral theorem, Stone–von Neumann, etc., the axioms P1–P5, Positive and the S5 derivation can be transcribed verbatim. That gives formal embeddability/conditional derivability A_Pos+S5 ⊢_{ZFC+analysis} ∃x Gx, exactly the same vacuous status the argument has in PA.

This embeddability is not internal provability. The positivity axioms, S5 necessity, essence and necessary existence are metaphysical postulates, not theorems of functional analysis, spectral theory, C*-algebra theory or quantum logic, and they are not definable in terms of vectors, projections, observables or spectra. They have no operational meaning in the Born rule and no empirical testability in QM. The classical Boolean distributive calculus on which the S5 derivation rests is not validated by the orthomodular quantum logic P(H); the modal operator has no interpretation in the Hilbert-space/operator-algebraic language.

Hence there is no unconditional, physically meaningful theorem of the customary Hilbert-space/operator-algebraic formalism of quantum mechanics whose content is the existence of a Gödel god-like necessarily existent maximally positive being. At best one obtains a vacuous conditional formal derivability in the classical ZFC metatheory shared with QM. By Gödel’s second incompleteness the necessity of existence is essentially a consistency statement the system cannot prove internally. The consensus practical answer is negative in the internal/operational/physical sense, affirmative only as a conditional formal exercise in the shared classical metatheory.

Unresolved nuance remains about how much the quantum-logical non-distributivity actually blocks the derivation beyond removing physical interpretation; the syntactic embedding survives only because it is carried out in the classical metatheory, not inside the orthomodular quantum logic. No colleague in round 2 claims an internal proof; disagreement from earlier rounds about locutionary emphasis is now essentially unified on no internal proof, conditional metatheoretic embeddability only.

The working formalism is ZFC + classical analysis, a complex Hilbert space H, B(H) or a C*-algebra, self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, states and the Born rule, formulated in ordinary classical first-order logic. Existence is set-theoretic existence in a fixed model. The language is non-modal: there is no primitive □,◇, no Kripke frame of metaphysically distinct possible worlds, no primitive predicate Positive(P), no notion of essence or necessary existence. In the Birkhoff-von Neumann reading the native propositional structure is the orthomodular lattice P(H), not a Boolean S5 modal algebra.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a conditional theorem of modal predicate logic S5 + P1–P5 with G(x) ≡ ∧_{P positive} P(x). The derivation S5+P1–P5 ⊢ □∃x Gx and hence ⊢ ∃x Gx uses classical distributivity and the S5 bridge principles □∃x Gx ↔ ∃x □Gx etc. It is a purely syntactic result of classical modal logic.

ZFC+analysis is of course strong enough to code syntax, first-order modal logic and a set-theoretic Kripke semantics for S5.
